exercises.objective: Recall the one-line core idea of three blocks from memory, without looking at the table.
exercises.prompt: Without looking at the table above, write the one-line core idea for MATH, DYN, and SYM from memory.
hints: MATH: think about what tools every later block borrowed from it (Taylor expansion, gradients, metrics, SVD).
DYN: think about the progression from equations of motion to control to stability.
SYM: think about the progression from propositional logic to relational/probabilistic representations.

exercises.objective: Apply the known-model-to-model-free spectrum to a concrete sim-to-real scenario.
exercises.prompt: A researcher has an accurate simulator (a full, known dynamics model) for a robotic arm, but the simulator doesn't perfectly match the real robot. Where would (a) using the simulator's model directly with LQR, and (b) fine-tuning with real-robot Q-learning data on top, sit along the known-model-to-model-free spectrum? Which approach would you expect to need less real-world data, and why?
hints: (a) sits at the 'fully known model' end (LQR, DYN-04): zero real-world data needed to compute the controller itself, but its performance is only as good as the simulator's match to reality.
(b) sits toward the model-free end, using real data to correct for whatever the simulator gets wrong, closer to RLEARN-01's residual dynamics learning or RL-03's Q-learning.

(a) needs less real-world data, by construction, but risks the sim-to-real gap producing poor real-world performance; (b) needs more real data but directly corrects for that gap. In practice this is exactly why RLEARN-01's residual learning and RLEARN-04's domain randomization exist: hybrid approaches that don't sit at either extreme.
